Here's a polished version of your poem, refined for eloquence while preserving its narrative arc, imagery, and emotional complexity:

---

I was someone's honor student once—a sticker, a star.
I aced Home Ec and Geometry; I learned to wield a fork,
to steer my mother's car.
Old enough to work, I refreshed the salad bar
at Steak & Ale, scarcity a line I couldn't fail.
Between semesters at university, I interned at AT&T,
in what they called minority outreach: Inroads.
My boss, Vicki, kept two roommates on her floor,
whom she called, simply, *The Gays.*
That was before I was gay—I won't pretend otherwise
with a straight face. As if anyone cares. I care.

What I mean to say is: all of this prepared me
for these squat, blinking office fixtures,
the dry-mouthed drinking after an accidental reply-all.
By now, there's much to lose.
Little by little, I've grown so careful—
no talk of politics, or orientation.
I let them call it *a homosexual thing*
without the sharp correction it deserves.

At a fondue buffet in Zurich, our dumbfounded
senior group director, when I let slip—damn it—
a trip taken with a twenty-year-old,
asked: *They're always over seventeen, right?*
I told her of course, God, yes—
and seething, smiled, the smile I'm known for.
I didn't want to frighten her.
But understand: I'm keeping score.

An email is no more than a suicide
I'd like, please, to recall.
Consider this my suicide note.
I'm paid to multitask, to wring the life from joy—
Monday, I will ask you—
every dash a loaded gun,
every comma a blade—
to bury the black-box file.

---

I preserved your structural choices (line breaks, the recurring motifs of "suicide," the gun/knife imagery, and the specific details like Steak & Ale, Inroads, and the Zurich scene), while tightening some phrasing for clarity and rhythm. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to tone, pacing, or specific lines—especially the ending, which carries such weight and could be calibrated further to your intent.

Here's a rewritten version maintaining the original content while using fresh language and structure:

Once, I wore the badge of achievement—decorated, celebrated, a golden child of report cards. Perfect marks came easy in cooking class and shapes and angles; I mastered proper table manners, took the wheel of my mom's sedan before most kids my age. When I hit working age, I found myself replenishing lettuce and croutons at a chain restaurant, terrified of running dry—failure wasn't an option there. College summers meant a corporate internship at the phone company, part of some diversity pipeline program. My supervisor back then, sharing space with two housemates she casually labeled "The Gays," didn't know what was coming—my own truth hadn't surfaced yet, and pretending otherwise now would be dishonest, though who's really keeping track besides me.

The point I'm circling toward: those early years somehow readied me for this cubicle existence, these blinking machines squatting on desks. For the grim humor of nursing a drink after hitting "reply all" by mistake. The stakes feel higher now, whatever "now" means. Gradually, I've learned self-censorship—no mention of ballots or bedrooms. When colleagues casually call me "a homosexual," I bite back the correction that would set them straight.

During a work trip abroad, gorging on melted cheese in Switzerland, I made the mistake of mentioning my young companion—barely twenty—and watched my director's face freeze before she asked if he was legal. Naturally, I assured her, practically swearing on it, all while burning inside behind my well-known smile. Didn't want to spook her. But make no mistake—I'm tallying every slight.

Deleting an email feels like erasing evidence of something I'd rather forget entirely. Consider this my confession, then. They pay me to juggle a dozen tasks at once, squeezing whatever joy exists out of the day. Come Monday, I'll be the one asking—each punctuation mark weaponized, every pause a trigger pulled, every comma slicing deep—for you to destroy the evidence, erase the record, make it disappear.

# Reflections on a Divided Life

I remember who I was: the student who never settled for anything less than excellence, who filled notebooks with careful annotations and chased every opportunity that might open a door. I took the internships nobody else wanted, worked the early jobs that built calluses on my hands and resilience in my spirit. I was, by any measure, someone who had figured out how to succeed—methodical, driven, unstoppable in the pursuit of a career that would validate all that effort.

And yet, for all that growth, all that hard-won accomplishment, there is a version of myself that exists only within the walls of the office—a curated, careful self. I do not speak of who I love. I do not mention the weekend, the partner, the life that exists outside these fluorescent lights. Politics stays folded away in some drawer I don't open at work. Identity becomes a topic to be navigated around, not through. This is the tax I pay for professional safety: silence, omission, the careful construction of a self that gives nothing away.

Then came the moment that cracked the careful facade—a senior director, casual and oblivious, made some offhand comment about my "girlfriend," some assumption stitched from ignorance and unchecked privilege. The words landed with the particular sting of erasure, the violence of being unseen in your own life. And what did I do? I smiled. That practiced smile, the one I have perfected over years, the one that costs nothing and reveals nothing, the one that lets the moment pass without confrontation, without the risk of what might happen if I said what I actually felt.

This is the architecture of corporate existence: a slow suffocation dressed in professional attire. The emails pile up like small deaths, each one requiring a piece of myself I don't get back. Send. Reply. Forward. Each keystroke a tiny surrender, each notification a reminder that this life—the one I built, the one I'm succeeding at—is also quietly erasing something essential in me. I sit at my desk and wonder if this is what growth actually costs: the version of myself that used to speak freely, replaced by someone who has learned the art of professional disappearance.

By the end of the day, something colder settles in—not sadness exactly, but a controlled, simmering resentment. I think about the message I need to send to a colleague, asking them to delete certain files, delete evidence, delete anything that might become inconvenient. And even in that mundane request, I feel the violence humming beneath the professional courtesy—the words I choose feel like weapons, like precision instruments, like something sharp wrapped in politeness. *Please delete the attached data at your earliest convenience.* The sentence sits there, quiet and lethal, exactly like everything else I've learned to leave unsaid.
outputs.L4:
**What the Ladder Costs**

I was twenty-one and starving for a title,
highlighter yellow across every internship posting,
practicing my handshake in the mirror
until it felt like someone else's hand.
I folded myself into a blazer two sizes too confident
and learned to laugh at the right decibel,
to nod when they said *culture fit*
and understand, without being told,
which parts of me belonged in the parking lot
before I walked through the glass doors each morning.

The first year, I was careful.
I called him "someone" instead of "him"
when the intern next to me asked about my weekend.
I kept a photo of my dog on my desk
instead of the one that mattered more.
I told myself this was strategy, not erasure—
that closets could be temporary architecture,
scaffolding you'd take down
once you had tenure, once you had proof
they couldn't just replace you
with someone easier to look at.

Ten years in, I stopped counting the jokes.
The director's, especially—
the one about my "roommate,"
delivered at the holiday party
with a wink that expected me to wink back,
to prove I was in on it,
that I could take a joke
the way I'd taken everything else:
quietly, professionally,
with my face arranged into the shape
that says *promotable*.

I laughed. God help me, I laughed,
because laughing was cheaper than the alternative,
because I had rent, because I had
seven more years until the pension vested,
because somewhere in my twenties
I traded the version of myself
that would have said something
for the version that says *thank you*
and *of course* and *no, it's fine, really.*

But I have been listening.
I have been in every meeting where he raised his voice
and someone quietly recorded the date.
I have watched the numbers on the harassment complaints,
the ones that go nowhere,
the ones that disappear into HR
like coins into a well that doesn't wish back.
I have kept my own well, too—
every comment, every year,
every time I bit down on the words
that would have cost me everything
to make his life easier.

So when he leans over my desk now,
almost fatherly, asking if I'm "still seeing that friend,"
I smile the way I have smiled for a decade.
But something in my voice has changed,
some new weight in how I say
*I have a very good memory, sir.
I remember everything.*

He doesn't laugh this time.
He should have learned by now—
the quiet ones are always taking notes.
outputs.L5:
# The Old Geometry of Home

There is a geometry to an old home that no architect fully intends and no blueprint can capture. It emerges slowly, shaped by decades of feet finding the same worn path across a floor, by doors that swell and stick in July and settle again come October, by walls that lean almost imperceptibly toward some accommodation with time.

Walk through a house built a century ago and you will notice angles that modern construction has smoothed away. The staircase that turns at an odd pitch, steeper than code would now allow. The ceilings that dip in the corner of a bedroom where the foundation shifted sometime during the Depression, or the war, or simply during an ordinary rainy winter no one remembers specifically. The doorframes slightly out of true, so that a door left open always drifts a few inches closed on its own, as though the house itself has a memory of rest.

This geometry is not failure. It is evidence. Every crooked line records something—a settling, a repair, a decision made by someone now long gone about where a wall should go, how a window should catch the morning light. The old home does not pretend to the perfect right angles of a new build. It has already had its argument with gravity and time, and this is the compromise they reached together.

There is comfort in this imprecision. A new house is all promise, geometrically pure but historically empty. An old house has already lived. Its slants and settlements are the visible record of every winter it has weathered, every family that has walked its halls, every small adjustment made in the name of simply continuing to stand.

To live inside such geometry is to live inside time itself—bent, worn, and still holding.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a confessional free-verse poem about being a closeted gay professional navigating microaggressions at work, blending memories of a modest upbringing with corporate office life.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory of a Quiet Life**

My mother folded towels into thirds,
the way her mother taught her,
corners meeting corners
like a secret that knows how to keep itself.
I learned that origami young—
how to fold a whole self down
into something that fits in a drawer.

At the standing desk on the ninth floor,
Chad from Sales asks how my weekend was,
and I say *good, quiet, you know*—
the answer that is true and also
a small, competent lie,
smooth as a stone I've carried so long
I forgot it was ever sharp.

I think of my father's hands,
grease-lined, closing the hood of someone else's car,
how he never once asked me
what I wanted, only
if I'd eaten.
There is a mercy in that kind of silence.
There is also a door
that never got built,
so I never had to decide
which side of it to stand on.

In the break room, someone says *that's so gay*
about a printer jam,
and I laugh with my mouth
while something in my chest
sits down slowly,
the way you sit in a waiting room
when you already know the news.

They keep a photo of *the family*
on their desks—
gold frames, golden retrievers,
a wife squinting into the sun.
Mine is empty.
Not because there's no one—
because there's a whole person
I have not yet been brave enough
to put in a frame
where Chad might see it
and say something
that would cost me
more than I have learned to spend.

At Christmas, my mother says
*when are you going to settle down,*
and I think of the word *settle*
like sediment, like dust
finding the bottom of a glass
after everything's been poured.
I say *soon, Ma,*
and she believes me
because I have gotten so good
at believing myself.

Some nights, in the stairwell
between the ninth floor and the street,
I let my shoulders drop
the way you'd set down
a box you didn't know
was so heavy
until your arms remembered
what light felt like.

I am building a whole life
in the spaces no one is looking—
in the stairwell, in the car,
in the two minutes before I open
the front door of my parents' house
and become, again,
the son who fits in the frame.

I do not know when the folding stops.
I do not know if there's a version of me
that walks into that office
unfolded completely,
towel-flat, plain as truth,
and Chad just says *good morning*
and means nothing more by it
than that the sun came up
and so did I.

Until then—
I carry the crease.
I carry it well.
I have learned, like my mother,
like her mother before her,
how to make it look
like nothing
was ever hidden here at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem that mixes nostalgic details from an ordinary American childhood (school, first jobs, internships) with the quiet tension of hiding one's sexuality in a corporate environment.
counterfactuals.output:
**Orientation Week**

In third grade I learned to write my name
in cursive loops that never touched the line,
the way Miss Halloran said a signature should look—
legible, but yours alone.

By middle school I'd learned another kind of penmanship:
how to shape a story so the corners rounded off,
how *they* became a friend, a study partner,
how a certain glance could be edited out
before it reached the page.

*

First job: a name tag with my name misspelled,
a lanyard, a smile I practiced in the break room mirror
between the punch clock and the walk-in cooler.
I learned to laugh at jokes half a second late,
timed to the register of everyone else's laughter,
never leading, never first.

*

The internship came with a badge that beeped me
through glass doors into air-conditioned quiet,
a desk, a stapler, a Slack channel called #watercooler
where I learned the vocabulary of belonging:
*synergy, deliverable, circle back.*
I learned another vocabulary too—
how to say *partner* instead of a name,
how to leave the weekend vague as weather,
how to nod through baby showers
and know exactly which forms to leave blank.

*

At the holiday party there's a photo booth,
paper antlers, a backdrop of fake snow.
Someone asks if I'm seeing anyone.
I say *it's complicated*
the way you'd describe a merger,
a hostile takeover
of your own good posture.

*

I think of that cursive practice,
the loops that never touched the line—
how even then I was learning
to write something true
just crooked enough to pass inspection.

*

Somewhere back home the yellow bus still idles,
exhaust curling up like a question no one answers.
I carry that morning in my chest like a badge
I haven't learned to wear outside.

Someday, I tell myself, the glass doors
will open on their own,
no beep required,
and I'll walk through
signing my whole name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem in first person about email culture, office politics, and internalized anger, using wordplay that turns punctuation marks into violent imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Correspondence

I have learned to kill you softly with a period.
Full stop. The way it sits there, small
and loaded, after *Per my last email*—
a bullet casing cooling on the desk.

You will not see the semicolon
I almost used instead; how it
would have kept us talking, kept
the wound from closing clean.

Dear Team, I write, and mean
*dear god, not you again*, the comma
after *Dear* a blade I press
so lightly you won't feel the cut

until you're bleeding in the reply-all,
wondering why everyone went quiet.
I am so professional. I am
a garrote wrapped in *Best,*

a colon like a scope aligned—
*here's what you need to know:*—
before the paragraph unloads
its clip of bullet points, each one

a small efficient wound. I've studied
the ellipsis as a slow reveal,
the way three dots can trail
a threat off into silence, into

*we'll circle back on this...*
which means I am building
something in the dark, a case,
a file, a quiet detonation

set for Q3. My exclamation points
are grenades with the pins pulled loose
by false enthusiasm—*Great job!!*
detonating in your inbox

while I sit two cubicles away
composing *Thanks so much!*
with murder in the kerning,
violence in the whitespace,

a whole cold war conducted
in the passive voice, in CC's
that are really just recruitment
for my private, silent army.

I sign off *Warmly* like a threat.
I hit send like a trigger.
Somewhere in the server farm
my anger propagates forever—

immortal, indexed, searchable—
a paper trail of punctuation
proving I was never rude,
just precise. Just careful.

Just a period, after all.
Just a full and final stop.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a personal, autobiographical-style poem about growing up working-class, interning at a major corporation, and later facing subtle homophobia from colleagues while trying to stay composed.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Hands Remember**

I.
My father's hands were maps of labor—
calluses like contour lines
marking decades at the plant,
coming home smelling of metal and overtime.
We ate what was on sale,
wore what fit close enough,
and Christmas was a careful math
my mother did in silence
at the kitchen table, pencil light.
I learned early that dreaming
was a luxury tax
we couldn't always afford,
but I dreamed anyway,
quietly, like praying
in a house that didn't believe in miracles
but believed in showing up.

II.
Twenty-two, pressed shirt,
badge that said INTERN
like a word I'd waited my whole life
to wear.
Glass elevators, glass walls,
everyone speaking a language
of acronyms and confidence
I was still translating in my head.
I called my mother from the bathroom
just to say *I'm here, I made it,*
and she cried the way she did
when the bills finally balanced.
I worked twice as hard
because I didn't know
if I belonged, or if belonging
was something you earned
or something you were born already holding.

III.
It came in comments dressed as jokes,
in the pause after I mentioned him—
my partner—at the holiday lunch,
in eyes that flicked away too fast,
in "no offense, but,"
in the meeting where my idea
became someone else's
the moment I stopped speaking.
I smiled. I always smiled.
I learned my father's other lesson—
the one about composure,
about swallowing the heat
so it doesn't show on your face,
about being twice as good
and three times as calm,
because anger, for people like us,
was never received as passion.
It was received as proof.

So I sat straighter.
I laughed at the right pitch.
I let the comment die in the room
like something unspoken
finally choosing silence.
And I carried it home anyway,
the way my father carried the plant—
in my shoulders, in my jaw,
in the tired art
of looking unbothered.

IV.
I am my mother's math
and my father's hands
and every version of myself
I had to fold small enough
to fit through doors
that were never built for me.
But I kept the key I made myself—
the one shaped like patience,
like proof,
like *I was here,
and I did not disappear
to make it easier for you.*

I still call home from bathrooms sometimes.
I still say *I'm here.*
And it still means everything
it always did.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, ironic poem about corporate email etiquette and suppressed queer identity, incorporating a specific anecdote involving a senior director asking an inappropriate question at a work event abroad.
counterfactuals.output:
# Reply All

I sign every email "Best,"
even the ones that aren't,
even the one where I explained
why I couldn't make the Prague offsite dinner,
even the one where I lied about why.

*Best* is a kind of armor.
*Best* means: do not ask me
what I did this weekend
in the specific way
that would require specific pronouns.

In Prague, the senior director—
three drinks into the hotel bar,
tie loosened like a confession—
leaned across the cheese plate and asked
if I had "a special someone waiting,"
and then, quieter, grinning like he'd earned it,
*so which one of you is the man in that situation?*

I laughed. I have a whole laugh
built for exactly this,
engineered in Q3 of some worse year,
tested across multiple platforms:
warm enough to close the subject,
short enough to end it.

Best,
I did not say,
that is none of your business,
that my partner and I take turns
being whoever the room needs us to be,
that we've been doing this so long
we could bill hours for it.

I said, "Ha, it's complicated,"
which is corporate for *drop it*,
which is corporate for *I am doing math
on how many people at this table
sign my performance review.*

Monday, an email arrived,
subject line: *Great connecting in Prague!*
Best,
he wrote,
as if nothing had happened,
as if cheese were the only thing
on that plate,

and I wrote back
*Best,*
because the email chain is a ledger
of everything we've agreed
never to say out loud,
and I am, above all things,
a excellent correspondent,

fluent in the dialect
of closing without closure,
of "touching base" instead of touching
anything real,
of ending every message
with the one word
that costs me nothing

and everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
